name: The Back Room: The Unfinished Fight
caption: The fight on the cover, finished at last. For five 7th-level characters.
description:
The party beds down in the back room of the Stickit Inn, and in the night the inn turns into somewhere else. On the road through it they meet the first party, each player's first-ever character, and the first party has one thing to ask: help us finish the fight on the cover of the 1977 Monster Manual. Three sessions: a road of puzzles and one fight, then the Cover in three waves, fought together.

Contents: 15 scenes; 25 actors; 33 journal entries; Monk's Active Tile Triggers automation. Shares its maps, art and audio with The Back Room; import one or the other into a world.

Start with the journal 00. The Unfinished Fight: Overview.

Bartleby Stickit, Bart to his friends (which is everyone who has drunk his cider twice). Keeper of the Stickit Inn, as his father was. Kind. Tired in a way that is not unhappy. He pours the house cider with a heavy hand, led the party up the stairs with a lantern and showed them the cots, and in the night he comes down the wrong stairwell with a tray.

Room 1. He tells them it is not morning yet and they should go back to bed; the road will be there tomorrow. He knows one detail about one character that the character has never told anyone. If pressed about it he does not understand the question.

Room 5. His voice from the common room below is the sound of ordinary morning.

description.value: Bartleby never attacks and cannot be made to. If attacked he sets the tray down, says 'well', and goes back up the stairs. He will have set a second tray by morning.

Once, in Room 1, he mentions one detail from a character's backstory that the player has never said aloud at the table: pick it from the sheet before the session. With nothing on the sheet to use, he asks after the character by the name the player almost gave them.

Asked whether he used to be a scrivener, he nods: 'But I'm not any more.' Asked why, or asked to write, copy, check or witness anything at all: 'I would prefer not to.' He says it pleasantly, every time, and goes back to wiping the mug.

text.content:
The Back Room: The Unfinished Fight

A three-session adventure for five 7th-level characters (it runs for 5th–8th). The party beds down in the back room of the Stickit Inn, and in the night the inn turns into somewhere else. On the way through it they meet the first party: each player's first-ever D&D character, the way the table remembers them. Those characters have one problem. On the cover of the 1977 Monster Manual there is a fight that was never finished, and they cannot finish it on their own.

The adventure is a road with stops, not a maze. Every door goes to one place, and back. Each stop is a puzzle, a fight, or both; each one has a Remnant in it; and the last stop is a long, hard fight in three waves, with the Remnants at the party's side.

If you ran The Back Room

This is the same module, maps, people and art, with a different route. Gone: the random Corridor doors, Misremembering, the visit count, the X door and its GM controls, the Corridor Between and the Echo. New: a fixed route (Crossroads, Cellar, Stable), a puzzle and a Remnant at each stop, the Hoard's request, and the Cover as three back-to-back waves fought together with the Remnants. The Back Room's own journals, scenes and tiles are untouched; import one adventure or the other into a world, not both.

The Route

2@UUID[Scene.TccuBe4B2jnBe1Jx]{2. The Common Room That Isn't}A room of roles. Find the real one. He hands over the X Map and the door unlocks.@UUID[JournalEntry.mfnJNCDH5bJdQgfd]{Fred the Fighter}

Doors. A door with a tile beyond it moves the whole party, and makes the next scene the active one. Some of those doors start locked: they open when the story says (the Remnant in that scene does it), and you open them the ordinary Foundry way: click the door icon (or right-click it to unlock). Each scene's journal says which door, and when.

Pacing

  • Session 1: the Stickit Inn, Room 1, Room 2. End when the guards step aside and the door opens on a crossroads at dusk.
  • Session 2: the Crossroads, the Cellar (one fight), the Stable, the Hoard. End on the ask, with the door to the Cover open.
  • Session 3: the Cover, all three waves, then the goodbyes and Room 5. Long rest before it, none during it.

The party can take short rests between stops in session 2, and should: the Cellar fight is meant to cost a little. They take a long rest in the Hoard before session 3 (the Remnants keep watch, and roll dice all night).

How to Run It: Step by Step

The whole adventure in order, with the Foundry pieces each step uses. Each scene's journal has the detail.

Three habits

  1. Doors move the party and switch the scene. The first character onto a door tile takes the whole party, and the new scene becomes active. Every door goes to one place; going back through it goes back.
  2. Locked doors open when a Remnant opens them. Room 2's door (Fred), the Cellar door (Thon), the Stable's east wall (T. Morlock), the Hoard's side door (the party says yes). You open each by clicking its door icon. Nothing else is hidden.
  3. People are already on the maps. Each Remnant is placed where the party meets them. In the Cover, the Remnants and the second and third waves' hangers-on are hidden tokens that the tiles reveal.

Before session 1

1. Check the modules

Required: Monk's Enhanced Journal, Campaign Companion, Monk's Active Tile Triggers. Recommended for sound: Ivan Duch's Music Packs, Michael Ghelfi, SoundFx Library, Adventure Music, SoundBard; and Patrol, for the barmaid.

2. Read the route

The overview, then the Hoard and the Cover journals: the end explains the beginning.

Use

Read @UUID[JournalEntry.Hgp8gyIeHlW2kcnc]{The Remnants}. Pick one secret detail from each character's backstory for @UUID[JournalEntry.h45zk7bUy2rjDVMJ]{Bartleby Stickit} to know (Room 1). Decide who the latecomer is, if anyone.

Doors are tiles. Walking onto one moves the whole party (every player character's token on the scene) to the next scene, and makes that scene active. Every door goes to one place; going back through it goes back. Monster and NPC tokens never set doors off.

Locked doors

Four doors start locked, with their tiles on the far side: Room 2's door (Fred's table unlocks it), the Cellar's east door (Thon's button six), the Stable's east door (T. Morlock walks through the wall), and the Hoard's side door (the party says yes). Open each the ordinary way: click its door icon; right-click to unlock first if needed.

GM controls

Hidden buttons in the top-left corner of a scene. Switch to the Tiles layer to see them; double-click one to fire it.

The CoverRorvik bursts inShows Rorvik at the cave mouth. Top of round 2 of wave 1.
The CoverWave 2 wakesShows the three outriders; reminder in chat. When wave 1's last monster drops.

Automatic tiles

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.jy79iM7p908gBS7t]{the vista} (a painted view of the place, no grid), then pull them to the map.

Room 1: The Back Room

The Stickit Inn sits where the Kettle Pass road leaves the valley, and everyone for three days in any direction knows its cider. @UUID[JournalEntry.rPX1OTMwmHlHXwnf]{Kael Shadowmere} in the corner booth has a job: ride guard on a lamp-oil wagon over the Kettle Pass to Thistlecross — three days, forty gold each, half now, leaving at first light (the handout The Job). The party takes it, and @UUID[JournalEntry.h45zk7bUy2rjDVMJ]{Bartleby Stickit} leads them up the stairs to the storeroom over the kitchen to sleep before the dawn road.

Why they're here

  1. It's on the road. The last bed and hot meal before three days of high road.
  2. The cider. Someone in the party has been promising the others a mug for weeks.
  3. The job brought them. Word went round: guards wanted for a wagon over the pass, ask at the Stickit Inn.
  4. They were passing through, and this is where night fell.

The barkeep goes up ahead of you with the lantern. A short landing at the top of the stairs, a door, and the storeroom: shelves of sacks and crocks, a cot for each of you already made up, one lantern on a hook, a small window over the yard. He tells you he'll have bread on at first light, and a jug of the house cider for the road.

Describe it in loving, mundane detail. Let them count the cots. The room has one door: the one they came in by. There is no other way out, and nothing to explore, which is the point: let them settle in, talk, and go to bed.

Keyed areas

  • A1. The landing. Top of the stairs down to the common room.
  • A2. The cots. One per character, blankets turned down.
  • A3. The shelves. Provisions, the party's receipts tucked under the crocks. Behind the far unit, at night only, a door.
  • A4. The window. Small, four panes.
  • A5. The stone. In the corner by the chest: a stone with a hilt in it.

The Latecomer

If a player arrives late, their character is the last guest of the night: Bartleby brings them up with a candle while the others are bedding down. If they arrive after night has fallen, they are the one who wakes.

Footsteps on the stairs, and a second light. Bartleby comes up with a candle and someone behind him, travel-stained, apologising. 'One more for the road, if you'll have them.' The last cot, you notice, was already made up.

Night Falls

When everyone is asleep, fire the GM control Night falls. Then pick the character whose player is most likely to get up and look: they wake.

The lantern is lit. Nobody lit it. The door to the landing is open a hand's width, and the stairs beyond it are stone, going down, too many of them. And behind the shelves, where there was a wall at supper, there is a door.

What the control did. Bartleby is now on the stairs (his token appears). The door behind the shelves (A3) is a real door now; it opens on the hayloft over the stable, and a ladder down. The stairs and the hayloft ladder now both lead to the same place: Room 2. Either way down is fine.

The stone. Whoever pulls the hilt draws a long iron key with no teeth (handout: The Toothless Key). It opens nothing. Keep it: it opens the door home in Room 5.

Bartleby, on the stairs

@UUID[JournalEntry.h45zk7bUy2rjDVMJ]{Bartleby Stickit} comes up the stone stairs with a tray. He is kind. It's not morning yet, he says; go back to bed, the road will be there tomorrow. He knows one detail about one character that they have never told anyone (pick it before the session). He is not a fight and cannot be made into one.

If they go back to sleep, they wake again in the dark, the lantern lit, and Bartleby has set a second tray. The way is down. Once anyone goes down the stairs or the ladder, the party is in Room 2.

Automation

Automated: GM: Night falls (top-left of the scene) shows Bartleby, opens the hayloft door and arms both ways down to Room 2. The stone opens the Toothless Key handout when clicked.

text.content:
Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.1GNykTLdI6a03pNS]{the vista} (a painted view of the place, no grid), then pull them to the map.

Room 2: The Common Room That Isn't

The Stickit Inn's common room. The fire is lit, the tables are full, and nobody is looking at you. In every booth, a hooded stranger. The barmaid is walking a slow circle between the tables with a tray and has not arrived at one. A drunk by the hearth is telling a joke to nobody. Two guards stand in the door.

Every patron is a role: a part in a scene, with one line, said the same way every time, whoever asks. The door out is locked, and the guards stand in it.

Keyed areas

  • B1. The booths. A hooded stranger in each, offering the job in the same words.
  • B2. The bar. Nobody behind it. Mugs of cider, every one pale gold. One is red.
  • B3. The hearth. The drunk: roll once on @UUID[RollTable.FQ9vCYjMtwTFn2km]{the Drunk’s Joke table} the first time anyone talks to him; that joke is his line forever.
  • B4. The door. Two guards. Locked.
  • B5. The stairs. Up to a landing, a door, and the bottom of the same stairs. Every time.
RoleTheir line
A hooded stranger (every booth)“Lamp oil, over the Kettle Pass to Thistlecross. Three days. Forty a head, twenty tonight, the rest on delivery. We leave at first light.”
The barmaid“Just coming, love.” (She never arrives. With the Patrol module she walks her circuit by herself.)
The guards (B4)“Move along. Nothing to see here.” (Both together.)
The merchant“Finest wares this side of the pass! Have a look!” (The table is empty.)
The old man“In my day, the pass was a dangerous road.”
The drunk (B3)His one joke (@UUID[RollTable.FQ9vCYjMtwTFn2km]{the Drunk’s Joke table}), forever.

The Puzzle: Who Is Real?

One patron is not a role: @UUID[JournalEntry.mfnJNCDH5bJdQgfd]{Fred the Fighter}, one player's first character (and quite possibly only ever a comic strip). He thinks it's mid-adventure and the party are his old companions. The puzzle is to find him and get him to say the thing everyone remembers him for: his Signature, POW!

Three clues

  1. He is the only patron who asks the party a question (“Ready for the next panel?”).
  2. His cider is red; every other mug in the room is pale gold.
  3. The player whose character he is will recognise him first. Let them sweat before they say so.

Getting the Signature

Anything that gets Fred to swing gets the POW: an arm-wrestle, a sparring bout, a dare, asking him to show how he fought the dragon, a fight with the guards. He never attacks the party. When the POW! hangs in the air in hand-lettered capitals, every role stops mid-line and turns to look at the party. Hold it for a beat.

The payoff

Fred hands over a map with an X on it (handout: The X Map): “The X is the way out. Everyone knows that. Follow it.” Click Fred's table (the tile under him): it shows everyone the map and unlocks the door. The guards step aside together without a word. Fred stays: “See you at the table.”

If they force it

If the party fights its way past the guards or breaks the door, let them. Fred catches up at the Crossroads, out of breath: “You forgot this!”, and hands over the map there.

Automation

Automated: click Fred's table when he says his Signature: everyone sees the X Map, and the door unlocks.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.lhxurR5AkL7lxs7y]{the vista} (a painted view of the place, no grid), then pull them to the map.

The Crossroads

The door opens on open country at dusk. A crossroads, a signpost, and long grass. Every arm of the signpost points the same way, north. The light is going, and it never finishes going. Someone is sitting at the foot of the signpost with his hood up.

@UUID[JournalEntry.KBUg4HBVJl1foHQz]{Strider} has been here a long time. He is never lost; he just has never had a map. Four roads lead out: north, south (the way they came in), west and east.

RoadWhere it goes
North (where the signs point)Back to the crossroads. They walk a few minutes and come in again by the south road.
SouthBack to the crossroads. They come in by the north road.
WestBack to the crossroads. They come in by the east road.
EastOn: a cellar door in a bank of earth. The Cellar.

The puzzle is only this: the signs lie and the roads loop. Let them try north first, everyone does. Show Strider the X Map and he reads it at a glance: “That's two doors from here.” He points east, and he is right (the Cellar door, then the Stable door, and the Hoard is through the next). The X on the map, when they look, is east.

Strider does not come with them. “Go on. I know the way now. I'll see you at the table.”

Doors

The four roads are tiles at the map's edges (the free-standing door frames). North, south and west loop back here; east goes to the Cellar. The Cellar's way back out comes in on the east road.

Automation

Automated: the north, south and west roads loop the party back to the crossroads; the east road goes to the Cellar.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.EiiueC7SiIeNdMvb]{the vista} (a painted view of the place, no grid), then pull them to the map.

The Cellar

A cellar, low and dry, and you know it: it is the back room from underneath. The same shelves, the same crocks, upside down on the ceiling-beams. Four provisions chests stand in the middle of the floor, your receipts still tucked under the lids. They are breathing. At the far end, a door, and in front of it a wizard with a heavy black rod, pressing a button.

@UUID[JournalEntry.LPETCYClp6EhxuAi]{Thon} has been trying to open the east door for a long time. It has no handle and no lock; nothing opens it (Strength, thieves' tools, knock: it is not locked, it is just shut). His rod will, as a battering ram. The trouble is the order.

The rod

Thon presses the buttons in order, one per press, one press on each of his turns, and names each one aloud: 1 mace, 2 flaming blade, 3 battleaxe, 4 spear, 5 ladder, 6 battering ram, 7 a pole that points north. He insists they go in order (“Hold on, I'll get there”). If anyone asks for the battering ram, or button six, by name, he grins, says “Button six!”, and presses it.

So the door opens on his sixth turn by itself, or as soon as someone listens to the list and asks for the ram. A party that pays attention gets out in two rounds; one that doesn't fights for six.

The chests

The first click wakes the @UUID[Actor.k958nZQMNZfvvOEx]{Provisions Chests} (four of them, already on the map). They fight until the door opens; then they stop where they are and are only chests again, and anyone stuck to one falls free. Thon will not fight them (“I'm busy”); he has a door to open.

This is the adventure's only fight before the Cover. It should cost a spell slot or two and some hit points, not a life. Let the party short rest afterwards; Thon shows them every button again while they do.

When the door opens, click its door icon to open it in Foundry. Beyond it is a ladder up, and the smell of hay. Thon stays: “See you at the table. Ask me about button seven.”

Doors

The door they came in by leads back to the Crossroads (by the east road). The east door is locked on the map until you open it; the tile behind it goes to the Stable.

Automation

Open the east door yourself (click its door icon) when Thon presses button six; the tile beyond it goes to the Stable.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.uS6nP4dRprQx5qYa]{the vista} (a painted view of the place, no grid), then pull them to the map.

The Stable

You come up the ladder into a hayloft, and look down into a stable. Horses in every stall, all of them facing the wall. They are your own mounts: the ones you never bought. High above, on a rafter, a halfling is sitting with his legs crossed, reading a sheet of paper.

@UUID[JournalEntry.5LVHv08PzaWG2vI8]{T. Morlock} is twenty feet up (his token is at elevation 20). Below, the stable has three doors: the hayloft ladder they came up, the big doors at the south end, and a small door in the east wall.

DoorWhere it goes
The hayloft (north)Back down to the Cellar.
The south doorsOut into the yard, round the side, up the outside ladder, and in through the hayloft. Every time.
The east doorLocked, with no keyhole. It doesn't open. The way on is through the wall.

Getting T. Morlock down

He will not come down (“Why would I come down? Come up.”). Someone has to climb to him: the posts are smooth, Strength (Athletics) DC 15, or a rope, a spell, a familiar. Or ask to see his sheet: he lowers it on a string, then the string, then himself, because nobody ever asks to see it.

When someone is up with him, or has read his sheet out loud (seventh level, every box filled in, climb walls ninety-nine percent), he drops twenty feet, lands on his feet, walks to the east wall, says “Elishaf”, and walks into it. There is a halfling-shaped hole. “Well? Come on.”

When he goes through the wall, click the east door's icon to open it: that is the hole. It stays open for a minute; the tile behind it goes to the Hoard. He does not come through after them. He is already there when they arrive.

Automation

Open the east door yourself when T. Morlock walks through the wall; the tile beyond it goes to the Hoard. The south doors loop back to the hayloft.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.t16LKTM7TWchd6PD]{the vista} (a painted view of the place, no grid), then pull them to the map.

The Hoard

A reading room: two tall arched windows of stained glass, timber ribs across the ceiling, books to the beams. Armchairs round a low table, dice on the table, still warm. Beyond it, through glass double doors, a smaller room lined with shelves, and in it, people you know. Fred. Thon. Strider. T. Morlock on the back of a chair. One chair is empty, and someone has put a character sheet on it anyway.

These are the Remnants, the first party, at their table. The empty chair is Rorvik's: he is late, as always. They are delighted to see the party, and they have been waiting a long time to ask them something.

Keyed areas

  • D1. The glass doors (south): the way in, and back to the Stable.
  • D2. The armchairs. Dice on the low table, warm, and a battered copy of the 1977 Monster Manual, face up.
  • D3. The portrait. Between the arches: a party of five, painted badly, in a cave.
  • D4. The inner room. The Remnants, at their own table. One chair empty, a character sheet on it.
  • D5. The windows. Stained glass: a red dragon, a unicorn, an owlbear, all mid-fight.
  • The side door (east wall): locked. It opens on the Cover.

The Ask

The Remnants explain, each in their own way, a line or two at a time. Let the players ask questions. The facts:

  1. The fight on the cover was never finished. The six monsters on the 1977 Monster Manual: a dragon, a unicorn, a centaur, a troll, a roper, an owlbear. Every time the first party got to them, the session ended. It got late. Someone moved away. “To be continued!” says Fred.
  2. Unfinished things don't end. That is what the back room is: everything left unfinished at a table. It catches parties, and it caught this one.
  3. They can't finish it alone. They are the ones who didn't. They need a party that finishes things. They need this one.
  4. Finishing it is the way out. The X on the map is on the cavern. When the fight is over, the back room lets everyone go, if they want to go.
  5. There is a hoard. Behind the monsters, the treasure pile from the cover. Each Remnant will give their own player something from it.

Why the party should say yes

  • It is the way home. The map, Strider and the Remnants all agree. Nothing else leads out.
  • They won't be alone. The first party fights at their side.
  • The treasure is real (After the Fight, in the Cover journal).
  • It's the players' own first characters asking. Let each Remnant ask its own player, by name. That is the hook; play it straight.

If the party refuses, the Remnants don't argue. They go back to their game, and the glass doors lead back the way the party came: Stable, Cellar, Crossroads, Common Room, and up the stairs to the back room, where Bartleby has set out a tray and it is still not morning. Every road comes back to this table. When they come back, the chairs are still there.

When they say yes

Thon gets up: “Allow me. Button six.” The side door bursts open. Click the side door's icon to open it; the tile beyond goes to the Cover. If the table wants a long rest first, they take it here, and the Remnants keep watch, rolling dice all night.

Automation

Open the side door yourself when the party says yes; the tile beyond it goes to the Cover.

text.content:
Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.I1OFkooks6T9bfO8]{the vista} (a painted view of the place, no grid), then pull them to the map.

The Cover

A dark cavern, and in it the picture from the cover of the Monster Manual, exactly as you remember it: a red dragon rearing over a pile of treasure, a unicorn, a centaur with a bow, a troll, a thing like a stump with tendrils, an owlbear. All frozen mid-fight. Fighting gaps: person-shaped spaces in the air where the adventurers stood. The gaps are your size. Behind you, the first party comes in, weapons out.

The party and the Remnants fight the six monsters together, two at a time: three waves, back to back, no rest between them. Each wave is a hard fight on its own for a strong party of five. The point is not any one wave; it is all three, in a row, with what they have left.

Keyed areas

  • E1. The cave mouth. Where the party and the Remnants come in. The roper's gap (the thief); the piercers on the ceiling above.
  • E2. The ledge. The centaur's gap (the archer).
  • E3. The hoard. The dragon's gap (the fighter with the shield), and the treasure.
  • E4. The chest. The troll's gap (the dwarf).
  • E5. The back wall. The owlbear's gap (the cleric); the unicorn's gap (the elf) beside it.
  • The back passage (west side): the way out, once it is over.

The Waves

WaveMonstersWakesIts trick
1@UUID[Actor.swDwYFmB0J7nU34p]{Troll (The Cover)}, @UUID[Actor.Fjvq8PRnpPIVOEra]{Roper (The Cover)}, six @UUID[Actor.GmQMZ2B6MBBsg8NF]{Piercers}The moment the party enters (the cave-mouth tile).The troll gets back up unless burned. The roper grapples from 60 feet and reels; the piercers drop on whoever it reels in.
2@UUID[Actor.jZeRhmifMxhHcBCq]{Centaur Captain (The Cover)}, @UUID[Actor.tyiNrAMmvaHRse7x]{Unicorn (The Cover)}, three @UUID[Actor.5TGdEuRtToUyrMgt]{Outriders}When wave 1's last monster drops: fire GM: Wave 2 wakes.Arrows from everywhere. The unicorn heals and shields the others, and can stand a downed monster back up: kill it first.
3@UUID[Actor.ftIjIMwENZwEuFwx]{Owlbear (The Cover)}, @UUID[Actor.5m3A4CR9yF4Cf2yp]{Red Dragon (The Cover)}, two @UUID[Actor.GVTu8D10Y9zNUJuy]{Owlbear Cubs}When wave 2's last monster drops: fire GM: Wave 3 wakes.The dragon breathes on the most people it can catch, Remnants included. The owlbear grabs and holds.

Between waves. When a wave's last monster drops, the next pair takes one round to finish its 1977 pose and turn around. That round is the only breath the party gets: drink a potion, stand someone up, move. No short rest.

The big six are visible from the start, frozen (their Still Fighting 1977 trait). Their hangers-on are hidden until their wave: the controls reveal them. Roll initiative once for the whole fight; add each wave's monsters when they wake, acting at the top of the next round.

If it goes badly

If two characters are down when wave 2 ends, wave 3 comes without the cubs (delete them from the scene). If the party is still fresh after wave 2, let the dragon open with its breath. Don't soften more than that: three hard fights in a row is the adventure.

Automation

Automated: arriving wakes wave 1 and shows the Remnants. GM controls: Rorvik bursts in, Wave 2 wakes, Wave 3 wakes.

The Remnants in the Fight

The Remnants are allies, and you run them. They are the first party, not the heroes: the players' characters finish this fight. One rule keeps them in their place:

  • Once per wave, each Remnant uses its Signature, and it always works (on each Remnant's sheet: Fred's POW!, Thon's rod, Strider's arrow, T. Morlock's vault and backstab, Rorvik's Hothead).
  • Every other turn, it Helps a character next to it (Advantage on that character's next attack or check), or Dodges. Describe it as the old party fighting the way it used to: shouting advice, a shield in the way.
  • It never takes the last hit on a monster.
  • It doesn't die. At 0 Hit Points it goes down, and stands up at the start of its next turn with half its Hit Points, mid-sentence. It has been in this fight before.

Rorvik

@UUID[JournalEntry.udLmhzBaYjJCWAe3]{Rorvik} isn't there when wave 1 wakes. At the top of round 2, fire GM: Rorvik bursts in: he runs in through the cave mouth, sword out. “Sorry I'm late. What did I miss?” From then on he acts first every round.

Speak for them. Each Remnant has a line for each wave on its Person page. Give each one a moment: the player whose first character it is should get to watch it do the thing everyone remembers.

After the Fight

The dragon goes down onto the hoard, and the coins slide. The cavern is quiet. The gaps in the air are gone. The first party stands there, breathing hard, looking at each other as if they had just remembered something.

The goodbyes. Each Remnant comes to its own player, one at a time, and says its last line (on its Person page): Fred's “We finished it. THE END.”, Strider's “This one's done.” Speak to the player, not the character. Then each one takes something from the pile and gives it to them:

FromTo their own player's character
@UUID[JournalEntry.mfnJNCDH5bJdQgfd]{Fred the Fighter}A +1 longsword (or the character's own weapon, made +1). The POW! still appears when it crits.
@UUID[JournalEntry.LPETCYClp6EhxuAi]{Thon}A wand of the war mage +1. It has one button, and it is labelled.
@UUID[JournalEntry.KBUg4HBVJl1foHQz]{Strider}A cloak of elvenkind, travel-stained.
@UUID[JournalEntry.5LVHv08PzaWG2vI8]{T. Morlock}A ring of protection, from his own finger. And, if they ask, his sheet.
@UUID[JournalEntry.udLmhzBaYjJCWAe3]{Rorvik}A pair of boots of speed. “You'll never be late.”

The offer. Then the Remnants say what they came to say: the fight is done, and anyone can go home now. Or anyone can come with them. The table is still up there, and there's a chair for everyone. “Come on. Last panel. Or the first one.”

The way out. The back passage (west side of the cavern) is open now. Its tile leads to Room 5: the back room, at dawn. The Remnants go ahead: they will be on the other side of the hayloft door.

If they flee mid-fight

The back passage is a way out at any time. A party that runs ends up in Room 5 having not finished it. Play Room 5 anyway: the Remnants are not behind the hayloft door, only the sound of a fight, still going.

Automation

Automated: the back passage turns off Room 1's night doors, locks its stairs door, and takes the party to Room 5.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.jy79iM7p908gBS7t]{the vista} (a painted view of the place, no grid), then pull them to the map.

Room 5: The Back Room, Again

The storeroom over the kitchen. Dawn light under the landing door, and through the small window, which is now a stained-glass window, the colours of the reading room laid across the cots. The cots are made. The lantern is out. The stone in the corner has no hilt in it.

The same Room 1 scene. They never left. Downstairs, ordinary morning: Bartleby calling up that the bread's going hard, the stranger's voice asking if they're up. And from behind the hayloft door, the Remnants, laughing (SoundBard: Remnants laughing, through the door).

The Choice

  • The landing door: home. It is locked. The toothless key turns in it. Beyond: ordinary stairs, fourteen of them, and the common room in the morning.
  • The hayloft door: the table. The Remnants, the low table, a chair for each character, dice still warm. “Oh, it's you. Go on through. They kept your seats.”

Making it a real choice

  • Each player chooses for their own character. Not a party vote. The party can split.
  • The price of going home: the Remnants are gone, and this time they said goodbye. The gifts from the pile come along.
  • The gift of staying: the game never ends. Every session is session one, with the people you started with. Say so plainly. It is not a trick.
  • Don't lean. No hint that one answer is right. Let the silence go on longer than is comfortable.
  • Make it physical. Each player moves their token to a door.

If they go home

The key turns as if the lock had been waiting for it. The stairs are wooden, and there are fourteen of them; you count. Bartleby is behind the bar, wiping a mug that is already clean. “There they are. Bread's hot. Jug's by the door.”

In the corner booth, the stranger has his hood down, checking the straps on a pack. “Wagon's in the yard,” he says. “If you're still coming.” Outside it is a cold, clear morning, and the road goes up into the hills one bend at a time.

Each character who goes home gains a level, and keeps what the Remnants gave them.

If they stay

The hayloft is warm and full of lamplight, and there is a low table up here, and chairs round it, and the people you used to be already sitting down. There is a character sheet on your chair, and the name at the top is the one you almost gave them. Somebody says, “Right. Where were we?”, and nobody remembers, and it doesn't matter.

The campaign ends here for that character, and it is allowed to be a good ending.

Then, The Last Word

When the last character has gone through a door, stop the scene's sound and start After the fight: Sad Strings (playlist Unfinished Fight: Music). Let it play a few bars. Then put the dice down and read The Last Word.

The Last Word

Close the campaign out of character: put the dice down, look up from the screen, and speak to the players, not their characters. There are two closings here. The first was written for this storyline; the second is the original Back Room closing. Read one, or the first and then the second.

For The Unfinished Fight

Every one of us left something unfinished at a table somewhere. A dungeon we never got to the bottom of. A dragon we never reached, because it got late, or somebody moved away, or the group just stopped meeting.

Tonight, our first characters got to finish theirs. And we were the ones who helped them do it.

That's the thing about this game. A story isn't over when we stop playing it. It's over when we decide it is.

So, for Fred, and Thon, and Rorvik, and T. Morlock, and Strider: we finished it. The end.

The original closing

Over the years, this game has been our interstice: our liminal space. We pause our busy lives, the ones where we hurtle from one thing to the next, and make room around a table to weave stories about things that don't exist.

After tonight it's back to the real world, and whatever the next destination is, good or bad.

There have been times when being in the back room, playing this game, was better than real life. There have been times, I think, when all of us thought it might be better just to stay in that back room.

But our time here is done now. Time to go back.

Then stop. Don't recap, and don't explain the ending. Let the table sit with it, and let whoever wants to say their first character's name one last time say it.

Bartleby Stickit, Bart to his friends (which is everyone who has drunk his cider twice). Keeper of the Stickit Inn, as his father was. Kind. Tired in a way that is not unhappy. He pours the house cider with a heavy hand, led the party up the stairs with a lantern and showed them the cots, and in the night he comes down the wrong stairwell with a tray.

Room 1. He tells them it is not morning yet and they should go back to bed; the road will be there tomorrow. He knows one detail about one character that the character has never told anyone. If pressed about it he does not understand the question.

Room 5. His voice from the common room below is the sound of ordinary morning.

Things They Say

  • Pouring. “House cider. Pressed in the yard, served cold. Goes down like water and gets up like a mule.”
  • Showing them upstairs. “Cot each, made up fresh. Bread on at first light, and a jug for the road. Mind the third step; it's been the third step since my father's day.”
  • The night, on the stone stairs. “Not morning yet. Back to bed, now. The road'll be there tomorrow. It always is.”
  • He knows (pick the detail before the session). “Your mother still keeps the lamp in the window, doesn't she? The blue one.”
  • If pressed about how he knows. “Know what, love? Drink your milk.”
  • If they go back to sleep. “There we are. I'll set another tray.”
  • Asked if he used to be a scrivener. (He nods.) But I'm not any more.
  • Asked why, or asked to write, copy or witness anything. “I would prefer not to.”
  • Room 5, from downstairs. “Are they up yet? Bread's going hard. Tell them the wagon's in the yard.”

A hooded stranger in the corner booth of the Stickit Inn, with a job and an untouched mug of cider. He gives his name as Kael Shadowmere, as if anyone could keep a straight face. Play it completely straight: the job is real, the pay is fair, the directions are good.

Room 2. There is a hooded stranger in every booth, and every one of them is a role, repeating the hook word for word. None of them is the Remnant.

Room 5. The stranger's voice rises from the common room below, asking Bart whether the party is up yet. The job is still there.

Things They Say

  • The hook. “Lamp oil, over the Kettle Pass to Thistlecross. Three days. Forty a head, twenty tonight, the rest on delivery. We leave at first light.”
  • Asked if it's dangerous. “It's a road. Roads have weather. That's the whole of it.”
  • Asked his name. “Kael Shadowmere. (He does not smile. Nobody ever believes him.)”
  • Asked why he's hooded. “It's cold in the booth.”
  • Room 2, every booth, word for word. “Lamp oil, over the Kettle Pass to Thistlecross. Three days. Forty a head…”
  • Room 5, from downstairs. “Are they up yet, Bart? We've a pass to cross.”

He introduces himself the way the strip's title panel did: 'FRED THE FIGHTER!' His player may not remember playing him. That is the point: he may only ever have been a comic strip, and he is here anyway.

Remnant. One of the first party: a player's first-ever character, as the table remembers them. Max Hit Points, never rolled. It never attacks first. It cannot answer any question about its past that is not its Signature. In this adventure it wants one thing: to finish the fight on the cover of the Monster Manual, which the first party never did.

The first party: each player's first-ever D&D character, as the table remembers them. They are not hostile. They have been trying to finish one fight since 1977: the one on the cover of the Monster Manual. They can't do it without the party.

This table's five: Fred the Fighter (Room 2), Strider (the Crossroads), Thon (the Cellar), T. Morlock (the Stable), and Rorvik, who is late. The three fallbacks stand in for a Remnant whose player can't make it, or for another table's first characters.

Rules

  • Max Hit Points, never rolled.
  • The Signature always works.
  • It never attacks first.
  • In the Cover: Signature once per wave, otherwise Help. At 0 Hit Points it stands back up next turn.

For another table

Ask each player privately: What was the first D&D character you ever played? Name, class, and the one thing everyone remembers about them. Don't say why. That one thing is the Signature. Put them at the stops in any order; give the latecomer's character Rorvik's entrance.
The Remnants' request: finish the fight on the cover of the 1977 Monster Manual, the one the first party never finished. It is the way out.

The Job

Wanted: four or five capable people to ride guard on a wagon of lamp oil from the Stickit Inn over the Kettle Pass to Thistlecross. Three days by the high road. Forty gold a head, twenty of it tonight, the rest from the chandler at Thistlecross on delivery. We leave at first light. Bring your own bedrolls; the wagon has room for packs. Ask for the one in the corner booth.

The pass is quiet this time of year. The road is good. Nothing about this is a trick.

The Toothless Key

A long iron key, drawn from a stone in the corner of the storeroom. It has a bow, a shank, and no teeth at all. It opens nothing in the room you found it in.

Keep it.

The Kettle Pass

What anyone in the valley could tell you, and what a traveller picks up over a mug at the Stickit Inn.

The road

  • The Kettle Pass is the only road over the hills between the valley and Thistlecross: three days by wagon, two on a good horse, one if you are a fool.
  • It takes its name from the Kettle, a round, steep-sided basin near the top where the road runs along the rim. On cold mornings the basin fills with mist to the brim and steams like a pot on the hob.
  • The road is old and well kept: stone-cobbled on the steep stretches, with mile-stones every mile and three way-shelters, a day apart, each with a roof, a fire-ring and a cord of wood that travellers are expected to replace.
  • The Stickit Inn stands where the road leaves the valley floor. It is the last proper bed and hot meal before the pass, and the first after it. Nobody remembers it not being there.

The trade

  • Thistlecross makes its living on wool, slate and lamp oil, and the oil goes over the pass in wagons all year. A chandler in Thistlecross, Old Wenna Marsh, buys every barrel the valley sends and pays on the nail.
  • Wagons hire guards for the crossing as a matter of course. Usually the guards are bored. Being bored is the job.
  • Stickit cider goes the other way: half the taverns in Thistlecross keep a barrel of it behind the bar and charge double.

The weather

  • The pass is quiet in the late season, before the snow. After the first heavy snow it closes until spring, and nobody tries it.
  • The mist in the Kettle can come up fast. The rule every carter learns from their mother: if you lose the road, stop, light a lamp, and wait. The road will be there when it clears. It always is.
  • The wind across the top sounds like voices if you let it. Carters sing to drown it out, and every one of them has a song for it.

What people say

  • There have been no bandits on the pass in living memory. There was a troll under the Kettle bridge once, in somebody's grandfather's day, and it was dealt with by four or five capable people nobody remembers the names of.
  • Count the mile-stones as you pass them. Everybody does. Nobody can tell you why.
  • The middle way-shelter has names carved into every beam, left by travellers over the years. It is lucky to add yours, and unlucky to look for your own.

The X Map

A map, drawn in a hand none of you recognise, of a place none of you have been: a crossroads, a cellar, a stable, a room full of books, and beyond it a cave. There is an X on the cave.

The X marks the way out.

system.gmNotes: The Stickit Inn, Room 1, Room 2. Night falls (GM control) once everyone is asleep. Fred is the real one in the common room; click his table when he says POW! End when the door opens on a crossroads at dusk.

The Crossroads (Strider reads the map: east), the Cellar (the chests fight until Thon presses button six; open the door), the Stable (T. Morlock walks through the east wall; open the door), the Hoard (the ask). End on the yes, with the side door open. Long rest in the Hoard.

The Cover, three waves back to back. Rorvik at the top of round 2 (GM control); wave 2 and wave 3 controls when the wave before falls. Remnants: Signature once per wave, otherwise Help. Then the goodbyes and gifts, the back passage, Room 5: home or the table.

tables.name: The Drunk's Joke
tables.description: Room 2, the hearth (B3). Roll once, the first time anyone talks to the drunk. That is his only line from then on, word for word, however many times anyone speaks to him. Nobody else in the room laughs.

results.description: A wizard, a fighter and a thief walk into a tavern. The barkeep says, ‘Is this some kind of quest?’ And the wizard says— (He laughs so hard he never says what the wizard says.)
How many adventurers does it take to light a lantern? (Beat.) None. It lights itself.
Fellow walks into an inn and asks for a room. Innkeeper says, ‘All we’ve got is the back room.’ Fellow says, ‘I’ll take it.’ Innkeeper says, ‘You already did.’
Knock knock. (He waits. If nobody says ‘Who’s there?’, he goes on waiting. If someone does:) Me. Still.
Did you hear about the barmaid? She’s been bringing me this drink since Tuesday. (He raises an empty hand.)
What do you call a door that always opens onto somewhere else? (Beat.) A door.
I told the hooded stranger a joke once. Now he’s in every booth. Went over very well.
Ten rats walk into a cellar. Farmer pays for them. Ten rats walk into a cellar.
What’s the difference between a stairwell and a staircase? (Beat.) One of them goes up. (He looks over at the stairs for a long time.)
Why did the halfling cross the high wire? To get to the far post. (Beat.) Which one’s the far post?
How do you know you’ve been at the Stickit too long? The cider tastes like the first time. Every time.
Best thing about this inn? Nobody ever leaves a bad word about it. (Beat.) Nobody ever leaves.
